questions.scenario: A report states: the 95 percent confidence interval for mean session time is 24 to 32 minutes. A stakeholder concludes there is a 95 percent chance the true mean is between 24 and 32.
questions.question: Is that interpretation correct?
options: No, it should say a 95 percent chance the sample mean is in the range.
No. The true mean is a fixed unknown; 95 percent refers to the procedure, meaning 95 percent of intervals built this way across repeated samples would contain it.
Yes, that is exactly what a 95 percent confidence interval means.
Yes, but only if the data is normal.
questions.explanation: In the frequentist view the parameter is fixed, so this specific interval either contains it or does not. The 95 percent describes the long-run success rate of the method, not the probability for one interval. The probability-about-this-interval reading is the Bayesian credible interval, a different object.
questions.misconception: A confidence level is a property of the procedure, not a probability about one computed interval. This is the classic interview trap.

questions.question: Holding the sample fixed, what happens to the width of a confidence interval as you raise the confidence level from 90 percent to 99 percent?
options: The interval gets wider, because higher confidence requires covering more possibilities.
The interval becomes a single point.
questions.explanation: More confidence means you must cast a wider net to be more sure of capturing the parameter, so the interval widens. There is a trade-off: higher confidence costs precision. You buy a narrower interval at the same confidence by increasing the sample size.
questions.misconception: You cannot increase confidence and precision at once for free. Higher confidence widens the interval unless n grows.

questions.scenario: You are estimating a mean from a small sample (n equals 12) and the population standard deviation is unknown.
questions.question: Which procedure is appropriate, and why?
options: The z-procedure, because it always applies.
The t-procedure, because with unknown population standard deviation and a small sample the t-distribution accounts for the extra uncertainty from estimating the standard deviation.
No interval can be computed with n below 30.
The t-procedure, but only when the data is uniform.
questions.explanation: When the population standard deviation is unknown and estimated from a small sample, using the normal (z) understates uncertainty. The t-distribution has heavier tails that widen the interval to reflect the estimated standard deviation, converging to the normal as the sample grows.
questions.misconception: Unknown population standard deviation with a small sample calls for the t-distribution, not the z.
